faq.q: What happens when a cell divides?
faq.a: The cell copies its DNA, shares out one full copy to each end, then splits into two identical daughter cells. This kind of division, used for growth and repair, is called mitosis.
asks: How does one cell become two?

faq.q: Why does a cell copy its DNA before dividing?
faq.a: Each new cell needs a complete set of instructions to work. Copying the DNA first means both daughter cells get all 46 chromosomes, not half each.
asks: Do both new cells get the same DNA?

faq.q: How are the chromosomes shared out?
faq.a: The doubled chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell. Protein threads called spindle fibres attach to them and pull one copy of each to opposite ends.

faq.q: How many cells are in the human body?
faq.a: An adult body has roughly 30 to 37 trillion cells, depending on size and how they are counted. Red blood cells make up the biggest share by number.
asks: How many cells do we have?
How many cells make a person?

faq.q: Do cells keep dividing when we stop growing?
faq.a: Yes. Even in adults, cells divide to replace worn-out ones, such as skin, gut lining and blood cells. The body makes millions of new cells every second, mostly blood cells.
asks: Why do cells divide after we stop growing?

facts: An adult human body contains roughly 30 to 37 trillion cells.
Human body cells have 46 chromosomes, which are all copied before a cell divides by mitosis.
The adult body replaces an estimated 3 to 4 million cells every second, mostly blood cells.
